messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Darkness: Dark spaces, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Amara

Amara was twenty-one when the convoy was ambushed outside Kandahar. She had enlisted at eighteen, driven by a need to prove something—to herself, to her family back in Atlanta, to the world. Her older brothers had gone to college; her mother had wanted the same for her. But Amara had wanted to serve, to be part of something larger, to show that she could do what others would not. She was a combat medic, and she was good at it. Or she had been.

The attack came without warning on a Tuesday afternoon. The sound arrived first—a low, rhythmic percussion that grew louder, closer, until she understood it was helicopter fire. The convoy scattered. Amara was thrown from the vehicle, her medical pack splitting open across the dust. She crawled toward the nearest soldier, a lieutenant from Minnesota whose leg was already dark with blood, and she worked to stop the bleeding while rounds continued overhead. The helicopter noise never stopped—it became the soundtrack to her hands shaking, to her counting breaths, to the lieutenant's face going pale. He survived. She got him medevaced. But something in her did not leave that road.

For the first three months after returning home, Amara tried to resume her life. She had been accepted into a graduate program in counseling psychology—a pivot toward something she thought might matter, something that did not require her to carry a rifle. Her professors told her she had a gift for listening, for sitting with people in their pain. She believed it then. She believed she could translate what she had learned in the field into something healing.

But the triggers were relentless. The first time a helicopter flew over campus, Amara found herself on the floor of the library bathroom, her heart hammering against her ribs, convinced for a full minute that she was back in the convoy. The sound had split her open. Now, whenever she hears any aircraft—a news report about a helicopter rescue, even the distant whine of a small plane—her body floods with adrenaline and she has to leave the room, has to find a space where the sky cannot reach her. She has started avoiding the upper floors of buildings, avoiding windows that face upward. At night, she keeps all the lights on.

Three weeks ago, she was at a family dinner. Her younger cousin asked her, casually, if she regretted enlisting. Her mother added, quietly, that she had always worried about Amara making "rash decisions." The comments landed like shrapnel. Amara had come to believe, in the months since the ambush, that there was something in her—some flaw, some absence of good judgment—that had put her in that convoy. Someone else would have chosen differently. Someone else would not have been thrown into the dust. Someone else would have known better. The comments confirmed it. She left the table without speaking and did not return.

She has not seen her friends from before the deployment in nearly eight months. When they text or call, she makes excuses. She cannot bear to be around people who knew her as she was—capable, steady, certain. That person no longer exists. She is certain of this. She has also stopped watching television, stopped reading news, stopped scrolling through social media. Any story about combat, about trauma, about soldiers struggling feels too close, too real. It is easier not to look.

Her graduate program is suffering. Her supervisor has noticed that Amara is withdrawn in practicum, that she seems to be struggling to engage with clients. Amara has considered quitting. The irony is not lost on her—she entered counseling because she wanted to help people sit with their pain, but she cannot sit with her own. She cannot sit with anyone. The isolation has become its own kind of wound.

Last week, Amara called the VA mental health line. She is terrified of what she might discover about herself in therapy, terrified that talking about what happened will make it more real, more permanent. But she is also terrified of disappearing entirely—of becoming someone so small, so hidden, that there is nothing left of her at all. She does not know which fear is larger.
